--- title: "Skill-Gap Analysis" subtitle: "Team Skills Compared With Analytics Job Postings in NAICS 5415" bibliography: references.bib toc: true execute: echo: true warning: false format: html: code-fold: true code-summary: "Show code" --- ## Purpose This page compares the skills requested in our analytics job postings with the current skills of our three team members. It answers two supporting questions from the Project Foundation page: - Where does the target user have skill gaps? - Which skills should the target user prioritize? We use our own team as three realistic examples of the target user: early-career candidates moving into analytics roles within Computer Systems Design and Related Services (NAICS 5415). ::: {.callout-warning} ## Data Limitation: Truncated Skill Lists As documented on the [Data Preparation](data_cleaning.qmd) page, the skill fields in the source extract were alphabetically truncated before delivery. **No skill name in the dataset begins with a letter after C.** Python, SQL, Excel, Tableau, Power BI, and R therefore never appear in the posting data, even though they are core analytics tools. To keep the analysis honest, we separate the skills into two groups: - **Market skills:** measured directly from our 287 job postings. - **Core tools:** added from outside evidence [@verma2019skills] because the dataset cannot measure them. Their demand is *assumed*, not measured. ::: ## 1. Team Skill Ratings Each team member rated their current proficiency on the course's five-point scale: | Score | Level | |:---:|---| | 1 | Beginner | | 2 | Basic knowledge | | 3 | Intermediate | | 4 | Advanced | | 5 | Expert | The skill list combines the most frequently requested skills in our postings with four core analytics tools. Each member also named the role they are targeting. | Team member | Target role | Background | |---|---|---| | Jenna | Business Intelligence / Business Analyst | Strong Excel and BI experience; some Power BI; beginner in coding | | Mariam | Business Analyst | Strong business and analytics understanding; beginner in coding | | Juan | Data Analyst, moving toward Data Scientist | Expert in Excel, Power BI, Tableau, and data analysis; intermediate in SQL and Python | ::: {#tbl-team-skills .cell tbl-cap='Self-assessed skill levels (1 = Beginner, 5 = Expert).' execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} skills_data = { "Name": ["Jenna", "Mariam", "Juan"], # Market skills (measured in the job postings) "Analytics": [4, 4, 4], "Business Intelligence": [4, 3, 3], "Business Requirements": [3, 4, 2], "Big Data": [3, 3, 3], "Artificial Intelligence": [2, 2, 3], "Algorithms": [2, 1, 3], "A/B Testing": [2, 2, 2], "Automation": [1, 1, 2], "Apache Spark": [1, 1, 2], "BigQuery": [1, 1, 2], "Airflow": [1, 1, 1], "Alteryx": [1, 1, 1], "Causal Inference": [1, 1, 1], # Core tools (not measurable in this dataset) "Excel": [4, 2, 3], "Tableau / Power BI": [3, 1, 2], "SQL": [1, 2, 3], "Python": [1, 1, 3], } df_skills = pd.DataFrame(skills_data).set_index("Name") CORE_TOOLS = ["Excel", "Tableau / Power BI", "SQL", "Python"] MARKET_SKILLS = [c for c in df_skills.columns if c not in CORE_TOOLS] df_skills.T ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ### Team Skill Heatmap ::: {#cell-fig-team-heatmap .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} skill_cmap = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list( "team_teal", ["#F3F8F9", LIGHT_BLUE, TEAL, NAVY] ) heat = df_skills.T # skills as rows, members as columns fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 8)) ax.imshow(heat.values, cmap=skill_cmap, vmin=1, vmax=5, aspect="auto") for i in range(heat.shape[0]): for j in range(heat.shape[1]): value = heat.values[i, j] ax.text( j, i, value, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=10, color="white" if value >= 3 else "#25353C", ) ax.set_xticks(range(heat.shape[1]), heat.columns) ax.set_yticks(range(heat.shape[0]), heat.index) ax.xaxis.tick_top() ax.tick_params(length=0) for spine in ax.spines.values(): spine.set_visible(False) # Thin white gaps between cells, plus a divider above the core tools ax.set_xticks(np.arange(-0.5, heat.shape[1]), minor=True) ax.set_yticks(np.arange(-0.5, heat.shape[0]), minor=True) ax.grid(which="minor", color="white", linewidth=2) ax.tick_params(which="minor", length=0) ax.axhline(len(MARKET_SKILLS) - 0.5, color=NAVY, linewidth=1.5) ax.text( heat.shape[1] - 0.35, len(MARKET_SKILLS) + len(CORE_TOOLS) / 2 - 0.5, "Core tools\n(not in dataset)", rotation=270, ha="left", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=GRAY, style="italic", ) ax.set_title("Team Skill Levels (1 = Beginner, 5 = Expert)", pad=28) save_figure("team_skill_heatmap.png") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Team skill levels. Darker cells show stronger skills; the lower block holds core tools that the dataset cannot measure.](skill_gap_analysis_files/figure-html/fig-team-heatmap-output-1.png){#fig-team-heatmap width=616 height=759} ::: ::: The heatmap shows three complementary profiles: - **Jenna** is the team's strongest member in Excel and business intelligence. - **Mariam** is strongest in business requirements and analytics understanding. - **Juan** has the strongest technical base, with intermediate Python, SQL, and algorithms. The lower rows of the market block are the shared weak spot. **No team member is above Basic knowledge in data-pipeline and cloud tools** (Airflow, BigQuery, Apache Spark, Alteryx) or in causal inference. ## 2. Skills Requested in Job Postings We extracted skills from the `SKILLS_NAME` field of the cleaned panel. Each posting stores its skills as a list, so we count **how many postings mention each skill** rather than total mentions. This stops a single long posting from inflating a skill's importance. ::: {#extract-skills .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} panel = pd.read_csv("data/processed/career_market_panel.csv") panel["skills"] = ( panel["SKILLS_NAME"].fillna("[]").map(json.loads).map(set) ) postings_with_skills = (panel["skills"].map(len) > 0).sum() skill_postings = ( panel[["ID", "skills"]] .explode("skills") .dropna() .groupby("skills")["ID"] .count() .sort_values(ascending=False) ) print(f"Postings with at least one skill listed: {postings_with_skills} of {len(panel)}") print(f"Distinct skill names: {skill_postings.size}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Postings with at least one skill listed: 1785 of 1790 Distinct skill names: 1394 ``` ::: ::: The first letters of every extracted skill name confirm the truncation described above: ::: {#cell-truncation-check .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} first_letters = pd.Series(skill_postings.index.str[0]).value_counts().sort_index() first_letters.rename("Distinct skills").to_frame().T ``` ::: {#truncation-check .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
skills A B C D E F G H I J ... O P Q R S T U V W X
Distinct skills 109 68 148 156 56 45 32 23 55 4 ... 33 113 16 77 184 78 19 15 20 1

1 rows × 24 columns

``` ::: ::: ### Most Requested Skills ::: {#cell-fig-top-skills .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} top_raw = (skill_postings.head(15) / postings_with_skills * 100).sort_values() fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6)) bars = ax.barh(top_raw.index, top_raw.values, color=TEAL, height=0.7) for bar, value in zip(bars, top_raw.values): ax.text(value + 0.8, bar.get_y() + bar.get_height() / 2, f"{value:.0f}%", va="center", fontsize=9, color=NAVY) ax.set_xlabel("Share of postings (%)") ax.set_xlim(0, top_raw.max() * 1.12) ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False) ax.set_title("Most Requested Skills in Analytics Postings (NAICS 5415)") save_figure("top_posting_skills.png") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The 15 skills mentioned in the most postings (share of the 278 postings with skill data).](skill_gap_analysis_files/figure-html/fig-top-skills-output-1.png){#fig-top-skills width=821 height=566} ::: ::: "Analytics" appears in roughly two of every three postings, far ahead of every other skill. The next tier mixes **business skills** (Business Intelligence, Business Requirements) with **technical data tools** (Automation, Airflow, BigQuery, Big Data). Employers in this industry want analysts who can understand the business problem *and* work with modern data infrastructure. ### Grouping Related Skill Names Many skill names in the source data describe the same capability ("Analytics", "Advanced Analytics", "Business Analytics"). We grouped related names into the skills our team rated, so that team ratings and market demand refer to the same thing. ::: {#tbl-skill-demand .cell tbl-cap='Market demand for each rated skill, after grouping related skill names.' execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} SKILL_GROUPS = { "Analytics": ["Analytics", "Advanced Analytics", "Business Analytics", "Analytical Skills", "Analytical Thinking"], "Automation": ["Automation", "Business Process Automation"], "Business Intelligence": ["Business Intelligence", "Business Intelligence Tools", "Business Reporting"], "Business Requirements": ["Business Requirements", "Business Analysis", "Business Process Analysis"], "Airflow": ["Airflow", "Apache Airflow"], "Big Data": ["Big Data", "Big Data Analytics", "Apache Hadoop"], "BigQuery": ["BigQuery"], "Algorithms": ["Algorithms"], "Artificial Intelligence": ["Artificial Intelligence", "AI Agents", "Agentic AI"], "Causal Inference": ["Causal Inference"], "A/B Testing": ["A/B Testing"], "Alteryx": ["Alteryx"], "Apache Spark": ["Apache Spark"], } demand = pd.Series( { skill: panel["skills"].map(lambda s, names=names: bool(s & set(names))).sum() for skill, names in SKILL_GROUPS.items() }, name="Postings", ) demand = demand.to_frame() demand["Share of postings (%)"] = (demand["Postings"] / postings_with_skills * 100).round(1) demand = demand.sort_values("Postings", ascending=False) demand ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## 3. Comparing Team Skills With Market Requirements Job postings list skills but not the proficiency level employers expect. To compare the two, we set a **target level** for each skill using a transparent rule based on how often the skill is requested: | Demand in postings | Target level | |---|:---:| | 20% or more of postings | 4 (Advanced) | | 10% to 19.9% | 3 (Intermediate) | | Under 10% | 2 (Basic knowledge) | | Core tools (assumed, not measured) | 4 (Advanced) | Core tools receive a target of 4 because the analytics-skills literature consistently identifies SQL, Excel, visualization tools, and a programming language as baseline expectations for analyst roles [@verma2019skills]. For each member and skill: - **Gap** = target level − current rating (0 if the member already meets the target) - **Priority score** = average team gap × demand weight, where the demand weight is the posting share for market skills and a fixed 0.5 for core tools The priority score favors skills that are both widely requested *and* weak across the team. ::: {#build-gaps .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} def target_level(share): if share >= 20: return 4 if share >= 10: return 3 return 2 targets = demand["Share of postings (%)"].map(target_level) for tool in CORE_TOOLS: targets[tool] = 4 demand_weight = (demand["Share of postings (%)"] / 100).reindex(targets.index) demand_weight[CORE_TOOLS] = 0.5 # assumed; see callout at top of page member_gaps = (targets - df_skills[targets.index]).clip(lower=0) # members x skills gap_table = pd.DataFrame( { "Skill type": ["Core tool" if s in CORE_TOOLS else "Market skill" for s in targets.index], "Demand (%)": demand["Share of postings (%)"].reindex(targets.index), "Target level": targets, "Team average": df_skills[targets.index].mean().round(2), } ) gap_table = gap_table.join(member_gaps.T.add_suffix(" gap")) gap_table["Average gap"] = member_gaps.mean().round(2) gap_table["Priority score"] = (gap_table["Average gap"] * demand_weight).round(2) gap_table = gap_table.sort_values("Priority score", ascending=False) # Saved for the improvement plan (Section 4) gap_table.to_csv("data/processed/skill_gap_table.csv", index_label="Skill") ``` ::: ### Where the Team Falls Short ::: {#cell-fig-gap-comparison .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} plot_df = gap_table.sort_values("Priority score") y = np.arange(len(plot_df)) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 7.5)) ax.hlines(y, plot_df["Team average"], plot_df["Target level"], color=LIGHT_BLUE, linewidth=3) ax.scatter(plot_df["Target level"], y, s=90, facecolor="white", edgecolor=NAVY, linewidth=2, zorder=3, label="Target level") ax.scatter(plot_df["Team average"], y, s=80, color=TEAL, edgecolor="white", linewidth=1.5, zorder=4, label="Team average") labels = [ f"{skill} *" if skill in CORE_TOOLS else skill for skill in plot_df.index ] ax.set_yticks(y, labels) ax.set_xticks(range(1, 6), ["1\nBeginner", "2\nBasic", "3\nIntermediate", "4\nAdvanced", "5\nExpert"]) ax.set_xlim(0.7, 5.3) ax.grid(axis="x", color="#E6ECEE", linewidth=0.8) ax.set_axisbelow(True) ax.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False) ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0) ax.legend(loc="lower right", frameon=False) ax.set_title("Team Average vs. Target Level (highest priority at top)") fig.text(0.01, 0.005, "* Core tool: target assumed from outside evidence, not measured in postings.", fontsize=8, color=GRAY) save_figure("skill_gap_comparison.png") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Team average (filled dot) against the target level (open ring). Each line is the distance to close; skills are ordered by priority score.](skill_gap_analysis_files/figure-html/fig-gap-comparison-output-1.png){#fig-gap-comparison width=765 height=724} ::: ::: ### Individual Gaps ::: {#cell-fig-member-gaps .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} gap_cmap = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("gap_gold", ["#FFFFFF", "#F2DDB0", GOLD, "#9A6B16"]) g = member_gaps.T.loc[gap_table.index] # skills (priority order) x members fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 8)) ax.imshow(g.values, cmap=gap_cmap, vmin=0, vmax=3, aspect="auto") for i in range(g.shape[0]): for j in range(g.shape[1]): value = g.values[i, j] if value > 0: ax.text(j, i, f"+{value}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=10, color="white" if value >= 3 else "#25353C") ax.set_xticks(range(g.shape[1]), g.columns) ax.set_yticks(range(g.shape[0]), [f"{s} *" if s in CORE_TOOLS else s for s in g.index]) ax.xaxis.tick_top() ax.tick_params(length=0) for spine in ax.spines.values(): spine.set_visible(False) ax.set_xticks(np.arange(-0.5, g.shape[1]), minor=True) ax.set_yticks(np.arange(-0.5, g.shape[0]), minor=True) ax.grid(which="minor", color="#E6ECEE", linewidth=1) ax.tick_params(which="minor", length=0) ax.set_title("Levels Needed to Reach Target (priority order)", pad=28) save_figure("member_skill_gaps.png") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Levels each member needs to gain to reach the target. Blank cells mean the target is already met.](skill_gap_analysis_files/figure-html/fig-member-gaps-output-1.png){#fig-member-gaps width=633 height=759} ::: ::: ### Gap Summary Table ::: {#tbl-gap-summary .cell tbl-cap='Skill gaps by member, ordered by priority score. Demand is blank for core tools because the dataset cannot measure them.' execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} gap_table ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ### Key Findings ::: {#findings .cell execution_count=12} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Top five priority skills: Python, SQL, Tableau / Power BI, Excel, Business Requirements Targets already met by the whole team: Analytics, Artificial Intelligence, Big Data, A/B Testing, Business Intelligence Total levels to close per member: Jenna 13, Mariam 17, Juan 9 ``` ::: ::: 1. **The team matches the market's most common request.** Analytics, the skill in about two-thirds of postings, is already at the Advanced target for all three members. Our business-facing strengths are real and relevant. 2. **The core tools are the biggest gap.** SQL, Python, and visualization tools are baseline expectations for analyst roles, and Jenna and Mariam are both at Beginner or Basic level in SQL and Python. Because the dataset cannot measure them, this finding relies on outside evidence, but it is the gap most likely to block a job application. 3. **Automation and pipeline tools are the largest measured gap.** Automation (about 28% of postings) and Airflow (about 17%) are requested often, and the whole team rates at or near Beginner. These reflect the data-engineering side of NAICS 5415, where Database Architects make up a third of postings. 4. **The team is complementary.** Jenna's Excel and BI skills, Mariam's business-requirements skills, and Juan's coding skills cover different parts of the market. Peer teaching inside the team is a realistic first step before outside courses. 5. **Juan is closest to the largest segment.** Data Scientists are 47% of postings and the highest-paid group (see [Market Baseline](eda.qmd)). Juan's remaining gaps are smaller and more technical, while Jenna and Mariam need a longer foundation in SQL and Python before those roles are within reach. ### Limitations - **Truncated skills:** Only skills beginning with A–C are observable. Rankings would likely change if Python, SQL, and other D–Z skills were visible. - **Assumed targets:** Postings do not state a proficiency level. The target-level rule and the core-tool weight are team assumptions, stated above so readers can adjust them. - **Self-ratings:** Team ratings are self-assessed and not independently tested. - **Small groups:** Business Intelligence Analysts have only five postings, so role-specific demand for BI roles cannot be estimated reliably. ## 4. Improvement Plan ::: {#plan-setup .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} import json import pandas as pd _MEMBERS = ["Jenna", "Mariam", "Juan"] _panel = pd.read_csv("data/processed/career_market_panel.csv") _n = len(_panel) _posting_skills = _panel["SKILLS_NAME"].fillna("[]").map( lambda s: set(json.loads(s)) if s.startswith("[") else set() ) plan = pd.read_csv("data/processed/team_skills_v2.csv").set_index("skill") plan["Demand (%)"] = plan["panel_skill_name"].map( lambda name: round(_posting_skills.map(lambda x: name in x).sum() / _n * 100, 1) ) def _target_level(share): if share >= 20: return 4 if share >= 10: return 3 return 2 plan["Target"] = plan["Demand (%)"].map(_target_level) _rows = [] for _member in _MEMBERS: for _skill, _row in plan.iterrows(): _rating = _row[_member] if pd.isna(_rating): continue _gap = max(_row["Target"] - _rating, 0) if _gap > 0: _rows.append( { "Member": _member, "Skill": _skill, "Current": int(_rating), "Target": int(_row["Target"]), "Gap": int(_gap), "Demand (%)": _row["Demand (%)"], "Priority": round(_gap * _row["Demand (%)"] / 100, 2), } ) plan_gaps = pd.DataFrame(_rows) _pending = {m: [s for s in plan.index if pd.isna(plan.loc[s, m])] for m in _MEMBERS} _pending = {m: s for m, s in _pending.items() if s} if _pending: pending_note = ( "Some ratings are still pending: " + "; ".join(f"{m} for {', '.join(s)}" for m, s in _pending.items()) + ". Those skills are left out of the member's priorities until they are rated." ) else: pending_note = "All three members have rated every skill on the list." ``` ::: This section turns the skill gaps into a plan. For each team member we identify the skills to work on first, suggest courses, certifications, and projects that close those gaps, and describe how the team can use its complementary strengths. ### 4.1 Setting Priorities We use the same rule as Section 3 to set a target level for each skill, based on how often it is requested in the postings. A skill in 20 percent or more of postings gets a target of 4 (Advanced), one in 10 to 19.9 percent a target of 3 (Intermediate), and anything less a target of 2 (Basic knowledge). With the v2 data every skill on the list is measured directly in the postings, so no targets are assumed. A member's gap is the target minus their current rating, or zero if they already meet it. Their priority for a skill is that gap weighted by the skill's share of postings, which favors skills that are both in demand and far from the member's current level. ::: {#tbl-plan-targets .cell tbl-cap='Target level for each skill, set by its share of postings.' execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} plan[["Demand (%)", "Target"] + _MEMBERS].sort_values("Demand (%)", ascending=False) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ```{=html}

Those skills are left out of the member's priorities until they are rated\. The pattern is clear: all three members share the same top priorities. Python, SQL, and data pipelines are both the most requested skills in the postings and the team's largest gaps, so the plan below is built around studying them together rather than as three separate plans. ### 4.3 Courses, Certifications, and Projects Each project uses this site's own data, so practice time also improves the project. | Skill | Free learning | Certification | Practice project | |---|---|---|---| | Python | Kaggle Learn: Python and Pandas | Not needed at this stage | Recreate the Market Baseline charts from the panel in pandas | | SQL | Kaggle Learn: Intro to SQL and Advanced SQL | Not needed at this stage | Rewrite the panel's filtering steps as Spark SQL queries | | Data Pipelines | Data Engineering Zoomcamp by DataTalks.Club, self-paced | Databricks Certified Data Engineer Associate, later stage | Turn `build_panel.py` into a scheduled pipeline that refreshes the panel | | Databricks | Databricks Academy self-paced courses | Databricks Certified Data Engineer Associate (about \$200) | Run the panel build in a Databricks notebook | | Machine Learning | Kaggle Learn: Intro to Machine Learning;
